title: MCI — Practice Question Bank
description: AUTO-GENERATED by courses/mci/build.py from the reviewer quizzes and scenarios — edit the reviewer JSON, not this file.

questions.text: An MCI is BEST defined as:
options: Any incident where casualties exceed immediately available resources
Any incident with 10 or more patients
Any incident declared by a hospital
questions.explanation: The resource gap defines an MCI. A fixed number is only a local activation tier.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: A tour bus rolls over with 32 passengers aboard. All are accounted for. This is a(n):
questions.explanation: The number of victims is finite and known — a closed (contained) incident.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: An earthquake damages the regional hospital and cuts the main highway. This is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: Infrastructure damage = compound; unknown, growing victim numbers in an earthquake = open.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: Which pairing of disaster type and dominant injury is CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Earthquakes cause entrapment and crush; tornadoes cause penetrating debris and blunt trauma.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: Three days after a hurricane, several family members are found confused with headache in a closed house running a generator. Most likely cause:
questions.explanation: Generator use indoors after storms is a classic delayed killer — CO poisoning. Get everyone out and give high-flow O2.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: Pandemics are classified as which type of natural disaster?
questions.explanation: Epidemics/pandemics fall under the biological natural-hazard group.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: The MCI mindset shift is from:
options: Maximum care for each patient to the most good for the most patients
questions.explanation: MCI care rations resources to maximize survivors overall.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: Which phase of the disaster cycle includes MCI drills and stocking triage tags?
questions.explanation: Planning, training, exercises, and equipment caches are preparedness.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: The primary mechanism of death in a crowd crush is:
questions.explanation: Sustained chest compression prevents ventilation — traumatic/compressive asphyxia.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: A second explosion occurs 20 minutes after the first at the same scene. Your FIRST consideration is:
options: Intentional event with secondary devices targeting responders
questions.explanation: Repeat events suggest an intentional attack; withdraw, stage away, and coordinate with law enforcement.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: Three Patients, One Ambulance — Night call to a rural two-car head-on collision 40 minutes from the nearest hospital. You are the only unit; the next is 30 minutes away. You find three critically injured patients. Is this an MCI?
options: No — MCIs need at least 10 patients.
Only if a hospital declares it.
Yes — casualties exceed immediately available resources; declare and request resources.
questions.explanation: MCI = patients > resources. Three critical patients for one crew in a remote area is an MCI. Declare early so help starts moving. Pearl: Small numbers + few resources = MCI. Declare early, downgrade later.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: The River Is Still Rising — Flash flooding in a low-lying district. Dispatch reports 'about 12 people' stranded. As you arrive, more calls are coming in from adjacent streets; the bridge to the main hospital is closed. How do you classify this incident?
options: Open, compound — expect more victims and degraded infrastructure
questions.explanation: Victims are still appearing (open) and infrastructure is damaged (compound). Expect longer scene times, alternate destinations, and request swift-water rescue rather than entering water yourself. Pearl: Open + compound = plan for self-sufficiency and longer holds.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: Week After the Storm — Five days after a hurricane, your service is busier than during the storm: a chainsaw laceration, a dialysis patient with weakness and peaked T waves, an elderly woman whose home oxygen ran out, and a family with headaches. What is the KEY lesson?
options: These calls are unrelated to the disaster.
Disasters cause a delayed wave: CO poisoning, cleanup trauma, and decompensated chronic disease.
Storm injuries are over once the wind stops.
questions.explanation: Post-disaster mortality is driven by CO from generators, cleanup injuries, and loss of dialysis, oxygen, and medications. The family with headaches needs CO screening and removal from the home. Pearl: Ask every post-storm household: 'Is a generator running inside or near the house?'
questions.hint: Review Chapter 1: MCI Fundamentals & Types of Disasters.

questions.text: You are first on scene at a multi-vehicle pile-up with ~20 patients. Your FIRST action is to:
options: Establish command and send a METHANE report
questions.explanation: Command and communication come before treatment. The first crew sets up the incident.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: In METHANE, 'E' (the first one) stands for:
questions.explanation: M-E-T-H-A-N-E: the first E is Exact location; the last E is Emergency services present/required.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: Which element of METHANE tells incoming units the safest approach route and rendezvous point?
questions.explanation: A = Access and egress.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: CSCATTT places TRIAGE after:
questions.explanation: Command, Safety, Communication, Assessment, then Triage, Treatment, Transport.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: The best way to report casualty numbers early in an incident is:
options: Give an estimate with severity breakdown
questions.explanation: Early estimates let resources move. Refine numbers in later updates.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: You arrive and see 6 office workers collapsed in a lobby, no trauma, two seizing. You should:
options: Withdraw, isolate upwind, report a suspected chemical incident and request HazMat
questions.explanation: Multiple collapsed people without trauma = chemical until proven otherwise. Entering makes you casualty #7.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: Why are 10-codes discouraged in MCI radio traffic?
options: They differ between agencies and cause confusion
questions.explanation: NIMS requires plain language to ensure interoperability across agencies.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: In the first-due crew, the member NOT in command should:
options: Perform a rapid recon and global sort, feeding numbers to command
questions.explanation: Recon and global triage give command the 'N' for METHANE.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: Which METHANE element is MOST often forgotten and endangers incoming crews?
questions.explanation: Omitting hazards sends crews into fire, chemicals, traffic, or violence.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: A good follow-up update structure after METHANE is:
questions.explanation: CAN updates keep command and dispatch synchronized.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: The Pull of the First Patient — You arrive first at a bus vs. truck collision. A screaming woman with an open femur fracture is right by your door. Through the windshield you see at least 20 more people, some not moving. What do you do?
options: Splint the femur — she's right here.
Partner does a quick recon/global sort while you declare MCI, name command, and send METHANE.
Load her and transport to clear the scene.
questions.explanation: First-in doesn't get sucked in. The open femur can wait seconds; the scene can't run without command. Declare, report, request, then assign triage. Pearl: Your first radio transmission is the most valuable intervention you'll do all day.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: Build the METHANE — Gas explosion in a 3-story restaurant at 42 Harbor Rd, rear wall collapsed, smell of gas still present. Approx 15 casualties: 3 critical, 5 serious, 7 walking. Harbor Rd blocked by debris; access via Mill Lane. Your unit and one engine on scene. Which report is BEST?
options: 'Explosion at Harbor Rd, lots hurt, will update.'

'Major incident declared. 42 Harbor Rd, rear of restaurant. Gas explosion with partial collapse. Hazards: ongoing gas leak, unstable structure. Access via Mill Lane — Harbor Rd blocked. Approx 15: 3 red, 5 yellow, 7 green. On scene: 1 ambulance, 1 engine; request 6 ambulances, USAR, gas utility, police.'
questions.explanation: This hits every METHANE element in one concise transmission, including the critical hazard (gas) and the access change (Mill Lane). Pearl: If you can't remember METHANE, read it off the action card on your visor.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: Quiet Lobby — Dispatch: 'multiple people fainted in a subway station.' On arrival you see commuters coughing as they exit, several collapsed on the platform stairs, and pigeons dead near a vent. Best action?
options: Bring the patients to your ambulance immediately.
Stop, withdraw upwind, keep ambulatory exiting patients in one area, report suspected chemical MCI (METHANE) and request HazMat/decon.
Enter with a BVM and start triage.
questions.explanation: Multiple collapsed casualties without trauma + dead animals = chemical clues. Don't approach (Step 1-2-3), control the exiting crowd for decon, and report. Pearl: Dead birds and fallen people — don't be the next one down.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 2: First-Due: Size-Up, CSCATTT & METHANE.

questions.text: Which is a Command Staff position?
questions.explanation: Command Staff = Safety, PIO, Liaison. They report directly to the IC.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: The optimal span of control in ICS is approximately:
questions.explanation: 3–7 subordinates, with 5 considered optimal.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: A 'Medical Group' is named so because it is defined by:
questions.explanation: Groups are functional; Divisions are geographic.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: The person in charge of an ICS Branch is titled:
questions.explanation: Section–Chief, Branch–Director, Division/Group–Supervisor, Unit–Leader.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: A battalion chief arrives on scene. Command is transferred when:
options: A face-to-face briefing occurs and the transfer is announced
questions.explanation: Arrival alone does not transfer command. Brief, accept, announce.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: Unified Command is used when:
options: Multiple agencies share jurisdiction over an incident
questions.explanation: UC lets fire, police, EMS, and others share one set of objectives without surrendering authority.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: Which section would source extra oxygen cylinders and backboards for a prolonged incident?
questions.explanation: Logistics supports the incident with supplies, facilities, and equipment.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: An MCI supervisor is directly managing 11 ambulance crews. The ICS fix is to:
options: Ignore span of control in emergencies
Add a supervisory layer (e.g., group/division or unit leaders)
questions.explanation: When span is exceeded, expand the organization — modularity is the point of ICS.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: Who may immediately stop an unsafe act on scene without waiting for the IC?
questions.explanation: The Safety Officer has authority to halt unsafe acts immediately.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: An off-duty EMT drives to the scene and starts treating patients without checking in. This is:
options: Freelancing — an accountability and safety problem
questions.explanation: Everyone checks in and receives an assignment. Freelancers can't be tracked or protected.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: Who's in Charge Here? — At a warehouse fire with 14 burned workers, a fire captain and an EMS supervisor both arrive and each starts giving orders to the same ambulance crews. Police set up their own post across the street. What fixes this?
options: Unified Command: co-locate fire, EMS, and police commanders at one command post with one set of objectives; EMS crews report only through the Medical Group.
Each agency keeps its own command post.
questions.explanation: Multi-jurisdiction incidents use Unified Command. Unity of command for crews is restored by clear EMS supervision within the shared structure. Pearl: One incident, one command post, one plan.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: Too Many Radios — You're Medical Group Supervisor at a train derailment. 12 ambulances, 2 rescue teams, and a bus are all calling you directly. Best ICS move?
options: Appoint Triage, Treatment, and Transport Unit Leaders and a Staging Manager; units report to them.
questions.explanation: Span of control exceeded → delegate. Unit leaders each supervise a manageable number; you supervise ~4–5 leaders. Pearl: When the radio never stops, your org chart is too flat.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: The Handover — You've been IC at a 9-patient bus crash for 15 minutes. The EMS duty chief arrives and says 'I've got it.' What must happen?
options: Face-to-face briefing: situation, hazards, objectives, resources, org chart; chief accepts; transfer announced to all units; you take a new assignment.
Hand over your radio and leave.
questions.explanation: A formal transfer of command keeps continuity and tells everyone who's in charge. The outgoing IC usually stays in the structure (e.g., as Medical Group Supervisor). Pearl: Brief — Accept — Announce.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 3: ICS for EMS: Command Structure.

questions.text: Which task belongs to the Transport Officer?
options: Assigning destination hospitals and logging each departure
questions.explanation: Transport matches patients to vehicles and hospitals and tracks them.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: The Triage Officer encounters a patient with arterial bleeding from the thigh. They should:
options: Apply a tourniquet, tag, and move on
questions.explanation: Hemorrhage control is a seconds-long LSI permitted during triage.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: Where should ambulances wait until called?
questions.explanation: Staging keeps uncommitted units organized and out of the scene until the Transport Officer requests them.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: Who sets up the red/yellow/green zones of the treatment area?
questions.explanation: The Treatment Officer establishes and runs the treatment area.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: The best way for hospitals to receive MCI information is:
options: Each ambulance calls its own destination
A single Medical Communications Coordinator / hospital coordination point
questions.explanation: One voice prevents duplicate calls and gives an accurate picture of distribution.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: A crew arrives and asks staging 'Can we just go grab a patient?' The correct reply is:
options: No — wait with the vehicle until the Transport Officer calls you to the loading zone
questions.explanation: Self-dispatch breaks tracking and distribution.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: Dead victims at an MCI should generally be:
options: Left in place unless blocking access to the living
Moved immediately to the treatment area
Covered and put in an ambulance
questions.explanation: Leave in place: preserves resources, the scene, and identification.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: Which is NOT a role of the EMS Incident Commander?
options: Inserting an advanced airway on a red patient
questions.explanation: The IC does not provide hands-on care.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: The treatment area is full and nothing is leaving. The MOST likely failure is in:
questions.explanation: Treatment areas back up when transport and staging aren't moving vehicles efficiently.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: A transport log primarily ensures:
options: Every patient can be located — which unit took them and to which hospital
questions.explanation: Tracking reunites families, informs hospitals, and supports re-triage and accountability.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: You're Wearing the Orange Vest — The IC hands you the TRANSPORT vest at a 26-patient bus crash. Three hospitals: General (Level I trauma, 8 min), St. Mary's (community, 5 min), Children's (12 min). 4 red, 8 yellow, 14 green — including 3 injured children. Best distribution strategy?
options: Reds to General (trauma center) a few at a time, yellows split between General and St. Mary's, injured children toward Children's per capability, greens by bus with a medic to a less-busy hospital — all logged.
Hold everyone until you hear from all hospitals.
Everyone to St. Mary's — it's closest.
questions.explanation: Match severity to capability and spread the load. Nearby hospitals already get flooded by self-presenters. Log every departure. Pearl: Distribute, don't dump.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: The Triage Officer Who Stayed — Fifteen minutes into an apartment-fire MCI, the triage count hasn't been updated since the first report. The triage officer is found inserting an IO in a burned toddler. What's the problem and fix?
options: Triage has stopped: hand the toddler to the treatment area team, return the triage officer to sorting and reporting counts.
Make the triage officer the transport officer.
questions.explanation: When the triage officer treats, triage halts and untagged reds go unfound. Lifesaving interventions in triage are seconds-long only. Pearl: Triage touches for seconds, then moves.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: Staging Chaos — Mutual-aid ambulances keep driving straight to the scene, blocking the fire apparatus and the loading zone. Two crews have loaded green patients on their own and left. Best fix?
options: Close the road to all ambulances.
Let them continue — more transports is good.
Ask dispatch to cancel mutual aid.
Appoint a Staging Officer, set a staging location in the METHANE update, require check-in, and release units only on Transport Officer request.
questions.explanation: Staging restores flow and accountability. Self-dispatching units clog access and lose patient tracking. Pearl: Check in, keys in, crews in.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 4: MCI Officer Roles & Action Cards.

questions.text: The decontamination corridor is located in the:
questions.explanation: Decon happens in the warm (contamination reduction) zone.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: The treatment area should be:
options: Inside the hot zone for speed
In the cold zone, upwind, next to the loading zone
questions.explanation: Safety plus flow: cold zone, upwind, adjacent to the loading zone.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: Which part of the treatment area should be closest to the ambulance loading exit?
questions.explanation: Reds are transported first.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: Ambulances should move through the scene:
options: On a one-way loop: staging → loading zone → hospital
By reversing into the treatment area
Only after all patients are treated
questions.explanation: One-way vehicle flow keeps the scene moving and safe.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: A suspected pipe bomb is found near the treatment area. The minimum mandatory evacuation distance is approximately:
questions.explanation: ≈70 ft mandatory; ≈1,200 ft preferred outdoor evacuation per stand-off charts — move the treatment area.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: The helicopter landing zone should be placed:
options: In the cold zone away from the treatment area
On the access road used by ambulances
Next to the red treatment area
questions.explanation: Rotor wash throws debris; the LZ also shouldn't block ground flow.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: Which statement about zones is TRUE?
options: Zones can move as wind, threat, or structure changes
The cold zone has no hazards ever
questions.explanation: Re-evaluate zones continuously, especially wind in chemical incidents.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: Staging during a suspected terrorist bombing should be:
options: At the most obvious nearby parking lot
Out of sight, in a location checked for secondary devices
questions.explanation: Secondary devices may target predictable responder gathering points.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: The Wind Changed — Industrial fire with 18 casualties. Your treatment area is set up 150 m east of the plant. Twenty minutes in, a light breeze shifts and smoke begins drifting toward the treatment area. Two treatment staff start coughing. What now?
options: Hand out surgical masks and continue.
Relocate the treatment area upwind immediately, re-mark zones, and inform IC/Safety and Transport of the new loading point.
Close the windows of the ambulances.
Transport everyone at once to the nearest hospital.
questions.explanation: Zones move with the hazard. A treatment area in smoke creates new casualties among patients and staff. Relocate and re-communicate flow. Pearl: Check the wind every 15 minutes — tie a strip of tape to an antenna.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: Gridlock — At a stadium MCI, ambulances are driving in from three directions, parking wherever they can, and backing out past the green collection point. Two crews almost hit walking wounded. Best fix?
options: Establish one staging area on a single approach, a defined loading zone at the treatment exit, and a one-way exit route — communicate it to all units.
questions.explanation: Flow design solves congestion: one way in from staging, load, one way out. Pearl: Draw the flow on the hood of your rig, then put it on the radio.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: Second Bag — Fifteen minutes after an explosion at a bus terminal, a police officer reports an unattended backpack 20 m from your casualty collection point. Your action?
options: Evacuate the CCP and staff beyond the stand-off distance using cover, avoid radio use near the device, notify IC/police — continue care at the new location.
Ignore it — police will handle it.
questions.explanation: Assume a secondary device. Move people out of line-of-sight beyond the stand-off distance; let bomb technicians manage it. Pearl: Time, distance, cover — for bombs as for radiation.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 5: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow.
questions.topic: Scene Layout: Zones, Staging & Patient Flow

questions.text: Under START, a patient who walks to the designated area is tagged:
questions.explanation: Ambulatory patients are tagged Minor (green) and re-triaged later.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: A non-ambulatory adult has RR 32, radial pulse present, follows commands. START category:
questions.explanation: RR > 30 → Immediate.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: A non-ambulatory adult has RR 30, radial pulse present, CRT 1 s, follows commands. START category:
questions.explanation: The criterion is MORE than 30; 30 passes. Perfusion and mental status are normal → Delayed.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: An adult is apneic. After you reposition the airway, he begins breathing. Tag:
questions.explanation: Breathing only after airway positioning → Immediate.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: An adult has RR 18, absent radial pulse. Tag:
questions.explanation: Perfusion failure → Immediate.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: An adult has RR 16, strong radial pulse, but cannot follow simple commands. Tag:
questions.explanation: Altered mental status (can't follow commands) → Immediate.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: JumpSTART: a 4-year-old is apneic after airway positioning but has a palpable pulse. Next step:
questions.explanation: 5 rescue breaths; if breathing resumes → Immediate; if not → Deceased.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: JumpSTART: a 3-year-old has RR 12. Tag:
questions.explanation: RR < 15 → Immediate.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: JumpSTART: a 6-year-old has RR 30, palpable peripheral pulse, alert, deformed femur, can't walk. Tag:
questions.explanation: RR 15–45, pulse present, Alert → Delayed.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: JumpSTART: a 5-year-old responds to pain only with abnormal flexion (posturing). Tag:
questions.explanation: Inappropriate P (posturing) → Immediate.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: Which is NOT performed during START primary triage?
options: Asking the patient to follow a command
questions.explanation: CPR is not performed during mass-casualty triage.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: A night-time winter MCI. The best START perfusion check is:
questions.explanation: Cold and darkness make CRT unreliable — use the radial pulse.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: The Quiet Child — Apartment collapse. You find a ~5-year-old boy lying still, not breathing. You reposition his airway — still no breathing. You feel a weak radial pulse. Per JumpSTART, what do you do?
options: Give 5 rescue breaths (~15 s): if he breathes → IMMEDIATE; if not → DECEASED.
questions.explanation: Pediatric arrests are often respiratory; a child with a pulse may respond to ventilation alone. JumpSTART spends 15 seconds on 5 breaths — never full CPR. Pearl: Pulse + apnea in a child = 5 breaths before black.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: Thirty on the Dot — Train derailment. A man pinned by the legs (can't walk) is breathing 30/min, radial pulse strong, CRT 1.5 s, and answers 'yes' when asked to squeeze your hand — and does it. START category?
options: DELAYED — RR is not > 30, perfusion and mental status OK.
questions.explanation: START's cut-off is RR MORE than 30. He passes all three checks → Delayed. Re-triage: entrapment can become crush syndrome. Pearl: Know the cut-offs exactly: > 30, > 2 s.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: Green Who Turned Gray-Skinned — 45 minutes after a bus crash, a woman tagged GREEN at the walking-wounded point is now pale, sweaty, and says she feels faint. She has left-upper-quadrant abdominal pain. What does this teach?
options: Walkers can hide internal bleeding — re-triage greens; she now meets IMMEDIATE criteria (perfusion).
questions.explanation: START sorts by snapshot physiology. A splenic injury may present late. Re-triage the green area regularly with a medic assigned. Pearl: Greens need a babysitter with a stethoscope.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: Thirty-Second Challenge — You've tagged 9 patients in 6 minutes. The 10th, a middle-aged woman, is screaming with an open tib-fib fracture, RR 26, radial pulse strong, follows commands perfectly, bleeding is oozing (not arterial). What's your tag and how long should it take?
options: IMMEDIATE because of the open fracture.
DELAYED — tag in ~30 s; she's loud but physiologically stable; move on.
questions.explanation: Noise and gore don't change START categories. She passes RPM → Delayed. The silent patient behind her may be the red. Pearl: Loud is alive — go find the quiet ones.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 6: Triage I: START & JumpSTART.

questions.text: In SALT, which group is assessed FIRST after global sorting?
questions.explanation: Still casualties and obvious life threats are most likely to need LSIs.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: Which is a SALT lifesaving intervention?
questions.explanation: LSIs: hemorrhage control, airway (± 2 breaths for kids), chest decompression, auto-injector.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: A breathing patient obeys commands, has a peripheral pulse, no respiratory distress, hemorrhage controlled, and an open femur fracture. SALT category:
questions.explanation: All four YES but injuries aren't minor → Delayed.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: A breathing patient has no peripheral pulse but is likely to survive with care available. SALT category:
questions.explanation: Any NO + likely survivable → Immediate.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: Expectant patients should receive:
options: Comfort care and re-triage when resources allow
questions.explanation: Expectant is a resource-based decision; comfort care and re-triage are required.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: In SALT, an apneic child after airway opening should:
questions.explanation: Children: consider 2 rescue breaths before tagging dead.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: Which is the BEST place to attach a triage tag?
questions.explanation: Clothing is cut off in treatment; tags on clothing get lost.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: High over-triage rates in an MCI are associated with:
questions.explanation: Over-triage diverts resources from the truly critical (Frykberg).
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: A patient tagged yellow deteriorates in the treatment area. The correct action:
options: Re-triage to red, note the time, and inform the treatment/transport officers
questions.explanation: Update the category and time; communicate the change.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: Which statement about triage systems is TRUE?
options: SALT is only for chemical events
SALT includes LSIs and an Expectant category
Triage Sieve is only for children
questions.explanation: SALT integrates LSIs and Expectant; START has no Expectant step.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: Gray or Red? — Tanker explosion. 40+ casualties, 4 ambulances on scene, 15 min to the next wave. A man with ~90% full-thickness burns is breathing shallowly, unresponsive, weak pulse. SALT category now?
options: EXPECTANT — survival unlikely with current resources; comfort care and re-triage when resources improve.
questions.explanation: SALT's Expectant category exists for this scenario. Resources spent on him now cost several salvageable lives. Provide analgesia/comfort and re-triage as resources arrive. Pearl: Gray is 'not now', not 'never' — re-triage when the scene changes.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: The Lost Tourniquet Time — At the hospital, a red patient arrives with a tourniquet on his thigh. No tag notes, no time. Nobody on scene remembers when it went on. What scene practice would have prevented this?
options: Writing 'TQ + time' on the tag (and/or forehead) at application.
questions.explanation: Tourniquet time drives surgical decision-making. The tag is the record that travels with the patient. Pearl: TQ without a time is half a treatment.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: Red Area Overflowing — Your treatment area has 22 'red' patients and 3 yellows from a nightclub stampede. Transport is stalled. On re-triage, 12 of the reds are alert, have good pulses, no respiratory distress, and minor injuries. What happened and what now?
options: Over-triage is clogging the red area and transport; re-triage and re-tag downward so true reds move first.
Request 22 more ambulances and keep tags.
questions.explanation: Over-triage buries true reds and wastes transport. Re-triage corrects it — that's the system working. Pearl: Accuracy is a life-saving intervention.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 7: Triage II: SALT, Tags & Re-Triage.

questions.text: Which is the MOST appropriate intervention in the MCI treatment area?
options: Two large-bore IVs for every yellow
Routine spinal immobilization of all patients
Full secondary survey on every patient
Tourniquet and wound packing for hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Hemorrhage control changes survival; the others slow flow without proportional benefit.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: The nearest hospital is usually overwhelmed early because:
questions.explanation: Upside-down triage: the least injured self-present to the closest hospital.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: Which loading plan is MOST efficient?
options: Wait until all patients are treated
One red + one or two greens per ambulance; greens in bulk by bus with a medic
questions.explanation: Fill seats sensibly and move greens in bulk.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: A hospital receives 30 casualties in the first hour. Its likely total is about:
questions.explanation: CDC rule of thumb: roughly double the first-hour count.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: Which patient should be transported FIRST?
options: Penetrating torso wound with signs of shock
questions.explanation: Non-compressible torso hemorrhage needs a surgeon now.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: The main reason to log every transport is to:
options: Track each patient's location for families, hospitals, and accountability
questions.explanation: Tracking keeps patients from 'disappearing'.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: Which statement about hypothermia in MCIs is TRUE?
options: Insulating from the ground is as important as covering
questions.explanation: Ground contact steals heat fast; hypothermia worsens trauma coagulopathy.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: Hospital capacity during an MCI should be obtained:
options: Through the Medical Communications Coordinator / hospital coordination center
questions.explanation: A single channel prevents duplicate calls and gives accurate distribution.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: The Field Hospital Trap — Your treatment area has 8 reds. Two paramedics are attempting RSI on one red, another is placing a second IV on a stable yellow. Four ambulances wait empty at the loading zone. Best correction?
options: Transport yellows first since they're ready.
Load reds now with essential interventions only (airway positioning/adjuncts, bleeding control, decompression); do advanced procedures en route or at hospital.
questions.explanation: Idle ambulances + waiting reds = flow failure. Treat to the minimum that's safe for transport and move. Pearl: Empty ambulances are a red flag in the treatment area.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: Three Hospitals, One Plan — Subway derailment: 6 red, 10 yellow, 25 green. Hospitals: Central (Level I, 6 min — already receiving 15 walk-ins), East (community, 12 min, 10 free ED beds), Children's (15 min). 2 reds are children. Best distribution?
options: Greens first to clear the scene.
Hold all patients until hospitals call back.

Adult reds split between Central and the next trauma-capable hospital, pediatric reds toward Children's if stable enough for 15 min, yellows to East, greens by bus to the least-loaded facility — all via Med Comms and logged.
questions.explanation: Match capability, respect capacity, and protect the trauma center for those who need it. Central is already flooded by self-presenters. Pearl: Ask hospitals for capacity by color: 'How many red, yellow, green can you take?'
questions.hint: Review Chapter 8: Treatment Area, Transport & Hospital Distribution.

questions.text: You arrive to find 4 workers collapsed near a loading dock, no trauma. Per Step 1-2-3:
options: Do not approach; withdraw, report, isolate
questions.explanation: Three or more casualties without explanation = do not approach.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: ERG pages listing materials by 4-digit ID number are:
questions.explanation: Yellow = ID number; Blue = name; Orange = guide; Green = distances.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: In the NFPA 704 diamond, the blue section indicates:
questions.explanation: Blue = health.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: A placard with hazard class 8 indicates:
questions.explanation: Class 8 = corrosives.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: Which PPE level uses an air-purifying respirator?
questions.explanation: Level C uses APR/PAPR — requires a known agent and adequate oxygen.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: The most effective initial decon step is:
questions.explanation: Disrobing removes most contamination fast.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: Wet decon is especially indicated for:
options: Caustic exposures or visible liquid contamination
questions.explanation: Dry decon suffices for most; go wet for caustics/liquids/symptoms.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: A critical contaminated patient with arterial bleeding in the decon line should:
options: Receive LSIs (tourniquet) from protected staff during rapid gross decon
Wait at the end of the line
questions.explanation: Combine LSIs with rapid decon — never transport contaminated.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: Which statement about Level C PPE is TRUE?
options: Requires a known agent and adequate oxygen
questions.explanation: APRs filter ambient air; they don't supply oxygen.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: ERG green pages tell you:
options: Initial isolation and protective action distances for toxic-inhalation hazards
questions.explanation: Green = distances for TIH materials.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: Placard 1005 — A tanker on its side on the highway displays a placard: class 2, ID 1005. A faint pungent smell; a motorist downwind is coughing. Best first steps?
options: Open the valve to vent pressure.
Ask the coughing motorist to come to your ambulance.
Approach to read the bill of lading.
Stop upwind/uphill at distance, look up 1005 in the ERG yellow pages → guide (orange) → isolation/protective distances (green), isolate and deny entry, METHANE with HazMat request.
questions.explanation: UN1005 is anhydrous ammonia (a toxic-inhalation gas). The ERG workflow — yellow/blue → orange → green — gives the PPE and distances. Ambulatory exposed people should move upwind and disrobe/decon before coming near you. Pearl: ERG: find the number, read the guide, check the green distances.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: 200 Wet Commuters — A sprayer releases an oily liquid in a train station. 200 people exit, many with burning eyes, some vomiting. Fire is setting up a ladder-pipe decon corridor. Your mass-decon priorities?
options: Decon in order of arrival only.
Wait for Level A suits for everyone.

Tell everyone to remove outer clothing immediately; prioritize symptomatic and visibly contaminated for wet decon; separate ambulatory and non-ambulatory lanes; privacy, warmth, keep families together; triage after decon.
questions.explanation: Disrobing is decon step one. Visible liquid + symptoms → wet decon. Good crowd management (modesty, warmth, families) keeps people from self-evacuating contaminated. Pearl: If decon feels humiliating or freezing, people will skip it — design for dignity.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 9: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon.
questions.topic: CBRNE I: HazMat Recognition, PPE & Decon

questions.text: A subway passenger has pinpoint pupils, copious secretions, wheezing, and muscle twitching. Most likely agent:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic + nicotinic signs with miosis = nerve agent.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Atropine in nerve-agent poisoning is titrated to:
options: Dry bronchial secretions and easy breathing
questions.explanation: Secretions and work of breathing are the endpoints.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: A nerve-agent casualty is seizing and apneic. Antidote kit dosing:
questions.explanation: Severe poisoning: 3 kits rapidly plus a benzodiazepine; support ventilation.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Pralidoxime should be given early because:
questions.explanation: Oximes only work before aging occurs.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: A house-fire victim is hypotensive and unresponsive. Which antidote is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Smoke inhalation → consider cyanide toxicity → hydroxocobalamin.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Why are nitrites avoided in smoke-inhalation victims?
options: They induce methemoglobinemia, worsening oxygen delivery with CO poisoning
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin + carboxyhemoglobin is a dangerous combination.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: A factory worker exposed to a gas smelling of 'freshly mown hay' feels fine. You should:
options: Advise rest and observation for ~24 h for delayed pulmonary edema
questions.explanation: Phosgene causes delayed non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Which agent causes painless exposure with blisters appearing hours later?
questions.explanation: Mustard is painless at exposure; lesions appear 2–24 h later.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: A theater crowd collapses with pinpoint pupils, slow shallow breathing, dry skin, no twitching. Best treatment:
questions.explanation: Dry miosis with respiratory depression = opioid agent.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Most riot-control agent exposures:
options: Cause delayed pulmonary edema in all patients
Resolve within ~15–30 min after removal to fresh air
questions.explanation: Self-limited; watch asthmatics and enclosed-space exposures.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Chlorine causes early upper-airway symptoms because it is:
questions.explanation: Highly soluble gases react with moist upper airways immediately.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Morning Rush, Line 3 — A commuter train car fills with a faint vapor. On the platform: a woman with pinpoint pupils and runny nose only; a man drooling, wheezing, vomiting; and a teen seizing and cyanotic. All have been disrobed and decontaminated. Best antidote plan?
options: Woman: observe (± 1 kit if symptoms progress); man: 1 kit, repeat atropine to dry secretions; teen: 3 kits + benzodiazepine + ventilation.
questions.explanation: Dose by severity. Vapor-only mild miosis/rhinorrhea may need no injector; moderate → 1 kit; severe → 3 kits + benzo and airway support. Titrate repeat atropine to secretions. Pearl: Mild 1, Severe 3 + Benzo.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Pulled From the Apartment — Firefighters carry a 40-year-old man out of a smoky apartment fire (burning furniture/foam). He is unresponsive, BP 78/40, RR 6, SpO2 98% on the monitor. What's going on and what do you give?
options: Combined CO and cyanide toxicity — 100% O2/ventilation and hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV.
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry can be falsely reassuring with CO. Shock and coma in a smoke victim = cyanide until proven otherwise. Hydroxocobalamin doesn't cause methemoglobinemia — safe with CO. Pearl: Smoke + shock = think cyanide.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: The Hay Smell — After a chemical plant leak, 12 workers mildly cough and say they smelled 'freshly mown hay'. All have normal vitals and want to go home. Disposition?
options: Treat as phosgene exposure: rest, O2 as needed, transport/observe ~24 h for delayed pulmonary edema.
questions.explanation: Phosgene's latent period fools everyone. Exertion accelerates the pulmonary edema — they should not walk out, drive home, or exercise. Pearl: Hay smell today = wet lungs tonight.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 10: CBRNE II: Chemical Agents & Antidotes.

questions.text: Which bioterrorism agent requires airborne + contact precautions?
questions.explanation: Smallpox spreads by respiratory and contact routes.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: A cluster of previously healthy postal workers presents with severe pneumonia, shock, and widened mediastinum. Most likely:
questions.explanation: Classic inhalational anthrax; not person-to-person.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: An alert, afebrile patient has double vision, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing that is progressing downward. Suspect:
questions.explanation: Descending symmetric flaccid paralysis with clear sensorium = botulism.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: A patient exposed to radiation from a hidden source (no contamination) is:
options: Not radioactive — no risk to responders
questions.explanation: Exposure does not make a person radioactive.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: The most effective first step in external radiological decon is:
questions.explanation: Clothing removal removes most external contamination.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: A dirty-bomb victim has an amputated leg with arterial bleeding and is contaminated. Priority:
options: Tourniquet and trauma care now, decon as part of care
questions.explanation: Life threats first; radiation contamination is rarely immediately dangerous.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: Doubling your distance from a radiation source reduces your dose rate to:
questions.explanation: Inverse-square law.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: Potassium iodide is indicated when:
options: Radioactive iodine release threatens thyroid uptake
questions.explanation: KI blocks thyroid uptake of radioiodine only.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: Under EPA guidance, the dose guideline for lifesaving actions by emergency workers is about:
questions.explanation: ~25 rem for lifesaving/protecting large populations; higher only for informed volunteers.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: A patient vomited 30 minutes after a radiation exposure. This suggests:
questions.explanation: Early onset of vomiting correlates with higher dose.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: You receive a call about a white powder in an opened envelope at an office. Best initial action:
options: Shake the envelope to see contents
Isolate the area, keep the envelope still, wash hands with soap and water, notify law enforcement/HazMat
questions.explanation: Contain, wash, notify; prophylaxis only if testing confirms a threat.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: The Bus Stop Blast — A small explosion at a bus stop. A police officer's radiation pager is alarming. 7 casualties: one with a partial leg amputation and arterial bleeding, others with fragment wounds. Best approach?
options: Standard PPE; tourniquet and triage now; remove patients' clothing; limit time near the seat of the blast; notify hospitals of contamination; decon as part of care.
Withdraw everyone until radiation is mapped.
questions.explanation: RDDs injure mainly by blast. Radiation risk to patients and responders is usually low; treat life threats immediately, minimize time near the source, and decon by disrobing. Pearl: Dirty bomb = bomb first, dirt second.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: Fever and Pustules — A 30-year-old with 3 days of high fever and back pain now has firm pustules on the face, forearms, palms, and soles — all at the same stage. Your actions?
options: Ignore the rash — treat the fever.
Treat as possible smallpox: mask the patient, N95/PAPR + gown + gloves + eye protection, limit crew, notify medical control/public health, decon the vehicle.
questions.explanation: Synchronous centrifugal pustules including palms/soles = smallpox pattern. A single case is a public-health emergency. Pearl: Same-stage pustules on palms and soles → think smallpox.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: Seven Burned Hands — Over a week, a clinic sees seven scrap-metal workers with painful red skin lesions on their hands and nausea. No chemical history. Most likely explanation?
options: A lost radioactive source causing local radiation injury/ARS (exposure)
questions.explanation: Clusters of unexplained 'burns' + GI symptoms in people handling scrap suggest an orphan radioactive source (e.g., a medical teletherapy head). These patients are exposed, not necessarily contaminated. Pearl: Unexplained burns in a cluster = think radiation.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 11: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear.

questions.text: The most common mechanism of injury in explosions is:
questions.explanation: Fragments and debris injure the most people.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: Which organ is MOST susceptible to primary blast injury?
questions.explanation: Air-filled organs: lungs, TMs, bowel.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: A bus-bombing survivor with intact eardrums becomes hypoxic 6 hours later. This:
options: Is consistent with delayed blast lung
questions.explanation: Blast lung can be delayed; intact TMs don't exclude it.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: In TECC Direct Threat (hot zone), the recommended medical intervention is:
questions.explanation: Only TQ (and moving to cover) under direct threat.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: THREAT's 'H' stands for:
questions.explanation: Threat suppression, Hemorrhage control, Rapid Extrication, Assessment, Transport.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: A Rescue Task Force typically operates in the:
questions.explanation: RTFs enter cleared-but-not-secure warm zones with police protection.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: Which management is appropriate for suspected blast lung?
options: O2 and cautious fluids; caution with positive-pressure ventilation
questions.explanation: Avoid fluid overload and barotrauma/air embolism.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: Why should EMS staging be out of sight in a bombing?
questions.explanation: Responders and CCPs are predictable targets.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: Indirect Threat care includes:
options: Wound packing, chest seals, needle decompression, hypothermia prevention
questions.explanation: MARCH-based care when the immediate threat is suppressed.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: Hospitals near a bombing often receive which patients first?
questions.explanation: Upside-down triage.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: Mall Shooting — Minute 12 — Police report the shooter is pinned down in the east wing. The food court (west) has been cleared but not secured. 15 casualties are there. You are assigned to a Rescue Task Force with 4 officers. Your RTF priorities?
options: Wait in the cold zone until the building is fully secure.
Enter the food court with escort: rapid hemorrhage control (TQs, packing), airway positioning, chest seals; move casualties to the CCP; minimal time on each.
questions.explanation: RTF's job is warm-zone TECC and rapid extraction. Prolonged procedures expose the team; police manage the threat. Pearl: Stop the bleeding, get them out, keep moving.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: The Train Carriage — An explosive device detonates inside a crowded rail carriage. A 30-year-old is walking, deafened, mildly short of breath, with a ruptured right eardrum. SpO2 94%. Best management?
options: Needle decompression for all blast victims.
Treat as at risk for blast lung: re-triage, O2, monitor SpO2/work of breathing, transport for observation — communicate in writing.
questions.explanation: Enclosed-space blast + TM rupture + mild hypoxia = high risk of evolving blast lung. Keep him under observation; he may deteriorate hours later. Pearl: Enclosed blast, walking patient — still watch the lungs.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: Second Device — Twenty minutes after a car bomb, EMS and fire have clustered at a single CCP in a plaza next to a parked van with blacked-out windows. What should command do?
options: Relocate the CCP and staging away and out of line of sight; request police clearance of the van and the new site; disperse vehicles.
Move all patients into the van for shelter.
questions.explanation: Secondary devices are designed to kill responders at predictable gathering points. Relocate, disperse, and get bomb-squad clearance. Pearl: The second bomb is for you.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 12: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC.
questions.topic: Explosive & Hostile Events: Blast, Active Shooter, TECC

questions.text: A worker trapped under a beam for 5 hours is about to be released. Which is MOST important first?
options: IV normal saline before release with cardiac monitoring
questions.explanation: Fluids before freedom; monitor for hyperkalemia.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: Why is lactated Ringer's avoided pre-release in crush injury?
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia is the main threat at release.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: After extrication, a crush victim's ECG shows peaked T waves and widening QRS. Give:
questions.explanation: Calcium stabilizes the myocardium in hyperkalemia.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: Crowd crush victims mostly die from:
questions.explanation: They cannot expand their chests.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: The FIRST hazard control at a rail derailment is:
questions.explanation: Overhead lines and third rails kill rescuers.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: Floodwater depth that can knock an adult off their feet if moving:
questions.explanation: About 6 inches of moving water can knock a person down.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: A marathon runner collapses, confused, temp 41.5 °C. Best initial action:
questions.explanation: Cool first, transport second for exertional heat stroke.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: An unaccompanied 6-year-old at an MCI should be:
options: Identified, photographed, tagged, and kept supervised until a verified guardian is found
Released to any adult who claims them
questions.explanation: Reunification is a safety process.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: During a prolonged power outage, which patients are highest priority for proactive outreach?
questions.explanation: Technology-dependent patients deteriorate quickly without power.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: Under the Slab — Earthquake. USAR has reached a 35-year-old man pinned at both thighs under a slab for ~6 hours. He's talking, HR 110, BP 110/70. They're ready to lift in 10 minutes. Best plan?
options: IV/IO access, NS 1–1.5 L/h before release, cardiac monitor, have calcium/bicarbonate/albuterol ready; coordinate the lift with USAR; watch for arrhythmia at release.
Leave him until the hospital is ready.
questions.explanation: Prolonged compression of large muscle mass = crush syndrome risk. Pre-release saline and hyperkalemia readiness prevent the 'smiling death'. Pearl: Fluids before freedom.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: Gate 4 — At a concert, the crowd surges at a narrow exit. Security radios that people are 'stuck standing'. You see faces deeply purple above the barrier. First priorities?
options: Get event control to stop inflow and open alternate exits, relieve pressure from the edges/barriers, extract victims, open airways and ventilate, then triage.
Announce over the PA for everyone to stay still and wait.
Push into the center of the crowd to reach victims.
questions.explanation: Crowd crush is a pressure problem. Stop inflow, open egress, decompress from the edges, and ventilate the asphyxiated. Pearl: Fix the pressure, then fix the patients.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

questions.text: The Silent Ventilator — Day 2 of a regional blackout during a heat wave. Calls are rising: a home-ventilator patient whose battery is at 10%, an elderly couple in a hot flat, and a dialysis patient whose center is closed. Key lesson?
options: Disasters create medical emergencies through infrastructure loss — prioritize technology-dependent and heat-vulnerable patients, coordinate shelters with power and dialysis diversion.
Tell them to wait for power.
questions.explanation: Compound incidents turn chronic conditions into emergencies. Registries, early outreach, and power-equipped shelters save lives. Pearl: No power = new patients.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 13: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters.
questions.topic: Special MCIs: Collapse, Crush, Crowds & Natural Disasters

A formal written report weeks later

options: Tell them it's normal and will pass
Refer to professional mental-health support and peer support

questions.text: The three PFA actions are:
questions.explanation: WHO PFA: Look, Listen, Link.

questions.text: The Missing Three — End of a 38-patient bus crash. Tags issued: 38. Transport log: 33 transported. Released on scene: 1. Dead: 1. Hospitals report receiving 31. What now?
options: Do not terminate: 3 tagged patients unaccounted on scene and 2 transported patients not found at hospitals — re-sweep the scene, check the transport log against hospitals, search for self-evacuees.
questions.explanation: 38 − (33 + 1 + 1) = 3 missing on scene, and 33 − 31 = 2 missing in the hospital system. Reconciliation finds them. Pearl: Math is a patient-safety tool.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 14: Demobilization, Recovery & Responder Resilience.

questions.text: After the Night — Two days after a nightclub fire with multiple deaths, your manager proposes a mandatory 3-hour session where every crew member must describe their worst moments in detail. Best recommendation?
options: Replace it with Psychological First Aid, voluntary peer support, practical help, and follow-up checks; refer anyone with persistent or severe symptoms.
Give everyone a week off and no contact.
questions.explanation: Mandatory single-session debriefing is not recommended. PFA principles and voluntary, ongoing support are evidence-informed. Pearl: Offer support; don't force reliving.
questions.hint: Review Chapter 14: Demobilization, Recovery & Responder Resilience.
